episode_title: 282: The 'Free Lunch Metric' Revisited, Client Case Study - Dave Porter

real_qa.q: What is the Free Lunch Metric used by real estate investors to evaluate property quality?
real_qa.r: The Free Lunch Metric uses the percentage of students qualifying for free lunch in a local school district as a proxy for neighborhood quality. David Porter established a threshold of 50 percent: if more than 50 percent of local students qualified for free lunch, he would not invest in that area. He linked data from Zillow to greatschools.com to identify this metric and used it consistently across all his property purchases without ever violating this rule.
real_qa.requete: Free Lunch Metric real estate investing

real_qa.q: How much did David Porter pay for a 3000 square foot Indianapolis property purchased during the Great Recession?
real_qa.r: David Porter purchased a large five-bedroom family house in Indianapolis with 3000 square feet for approximately $80,000, which equaled about $29 per square foot. The property has since appreciated to approximately $350,000 in value, representing over a 4x return since the 2007-2008 purchase period.

real_qa.q: What is the recommended cash reserve buffer that Heroic Investing now requires for real estate investment properties?
real_qa.r: Heroic Investing has added a minimum 4 percent reserves requirement to their property investment performa. This means investors should earmark 4 percent of the purchase price as a cash cushion kept in the bank for emergencies, vacancies, and surprise repair items, ensuring investors are not forced to sell or get into trouble when unexpected costs arise.
real_qa.requete: 4% reserves real estate property buffer minimum

real_qa.q: How many properties did David Porter purchase in Indianapolis and Phoenix through Heroic Investing?
real_qa.r: David Porter purchased 16 properties in Indianapolis starting in late 2007 and early 2008, and 2 properties in Phoenix (specifically Gilbert) — one in 2011 and one in 2014. Combined with his pre-existing California rental properties, he built a total portfolio of approximately 22 properties across three markets.
real_qa.requete: 16 properties Indianapolis Phoenix real estate portfolio

real_qa.q: What maximum insurance deductible strategy does David Porter recommend for rental properties?
real_qa.r: David Porter switched to a maximum deductible strategy on all his rental property insurance, with deductibles ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 depending on the carrier and market. He adopted this approach to insure against catastrophic loss only, avoiding small claims that would trigger rate increases, and successfully reduced his overall insurance costs while never filing a claim across all his years as an investor.
real_qa.requete: maximum deductible insurance rental property strategy

guest.titre: Retired Real Estate Investor and Client
guest.bio_context: David Porter has worked in logistics and transportation for most of his career, with a brief stint in financial services during the global financial crisis. He began investing in real estate around 2007-2008 during the Great Recession, purchasing properties through Heroic Investing after hearing radio commercials. He is now partially retired, having built a portfolio of 22 properties across three markets (California, Indianapolis, and Phoenix/Gilbert) that he has held and never sold.
